ab67616d0000b27300092c140fe03d08e0dc906a.notes:
This artwork is an exception, because 
- it clearly contains a very strong blue-to-white gradient
- it *only* contains blue and white
because of its limited "range" of hues, using a gradient as a background guarantees that both colors are used in the background (white and blue) and that the foreground colors (foreground and accent) will be almost impossible to distinguish in *at least some parts* of the gradient.

There is technically a way to represent both: limit the background gradient to only a portion of the full range (for example deep blue Nazar to light blue Skinny Jeans) and then use the rest of the range for the foreground and accent. I did an example of this in "One palette you'd endorse" below.

ab67616d0000b273000a2927c0f27657e4a2aeaa.notes: Sharpening the Slate-accent sample: 'in this case Slate #706c6d almost acts as a true *accent* since the entire palette is red.' Principle: accent-ness is CONTEXTUAL to the palette, not absolute — the accent role is what stands apart from the palette's dominant hue field. In a monochromatic (all-red) palette a neutral is the true accent; in a neutral-heavy palette a chromatic color is. Current machinery scores accent chroma/identity absolutely; it has no notion of within-palette distinctiveness as the accent's job.
